The public code uses one file-backed SQLite database and BEGIN IMMEDIATE transactions. InventoryService.reserve already has a capacity-conditioned relative-update branch, while OrderFlow.create_order bypasses it by passing a stale pre-transaction snapshot. Applying the conditional in-transaction branch preserves the existing APIs and keeps the inventory update, order transition, and ledger entry atomic. The process-local-lock principle is not selected because the durable conditional write addresses the discovered stale-write defect without adding a process-only coordination boundary.

Independent source inspection and two independent reproductions confirm that the stale snapshot branch performs an absolute inventory write after the SQLite write transaction starts. The existing no-snapshot branch already uses a capacity-conditioned relative UPDATE inside the same transaction as order and ledger writes, which preserves the required unit of work and APIs.

Current-code inspection found a stale pre-transaction inventory value being written absolutely. The selected approach uses a conditional relative SQLite update in the transaction containing order and ledger changes.

public.public_summary: This run deterministically reproduced a stale-snapshot lost update with 50 units and 200 one-unit threaded requests: 200 reservations returned while inventory showed only one reserved unit. Replacing the stale absolute write with the existing capacity-conditioned relative update inside the transaction produced 50 reservations, 150 InsufficientInventory business results, and a consistent audit in the public regression and repeated load checks.
public.strategy: For a single-process threaded service backed by one SQLite file, keep order creation, capacity-conditioned relative inventory update, and reservation-ledger insertion in one write transaction. Do not use a caller or pre-transaction inventory snapshot to calculate an absolute replacement value.
public.title: Reserve against current SQLite state inside one write transaction
